title: Action Learning for Scientific Simulations
authors: Sarah Liaw, Yuanqi Du, Yilun Du
abstract: Understanding and controlling how systems evolve is central to science and engineering, where many problems require reasoning about complete trajectories. Existing approaches typically learn local dynamics or generate trajectories, but objectives constructed from individual transitions can miss dependencies across time, while generative models do not necessarily provide a tractable objective for evaluating and optimizing arbitrary paths. We study $\textit{action learning}$, the problem of recovering a stochastic action from trajectory observations, yielding a common objective for reasoning about dynamical systems. We introduce $\textbf{LEAP}$ ($\textbf{L}$earned $\textbf{E}$nergy on $\textbf{A}$ction $\textbf{P}$aths), which anchors the unknown action to a tractable reference process and learns the remaining correction by comparing observed trajectories with reference trajectories. This construction yields a differentiable objective on path space that can capture both local dynamical structure and nonadditive dependencies across time. Once learned, the same action can be flexibly reused for path ranking and inference, mechanism steering, constrained optimization and sampling. Across stochastic physical systems, many-body orbital dynamics and molecular simulations, LEAP recovers underlying dynamics, captures dependencies across time and enables transfer across inference objectives and physical conditions. We show that $\textit{action learning}$ is a promising framework for turning trajectory observations into reusable objectives for scientific inference and control.

infographic.key_insight: LEAP learns a reusable, differentiable objective over complete trajectories, capturing local dynamics and dependencies across time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A single learned action can support trajectory ranking, inference, mechanism steering, constrained optimization and sampling in scientific simulations.
method: Anchor the unknown stochastic action to a tractable reference process.
Learn an action correction by comparing observed trajectories with reference trajectories.
Reuse the resulting path-space objective across inference and control tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations span stochastic physical systems, many-body orbital dynamics and molecular simulations, reporting dynamics recovery, temporal dependency capture and transfer across objectives and physical conditions.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify accuracy or computational cost, leaving practical scaling and reference-process sensitivity to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: Action Learning for Scientific Simulations

title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing
authors: Isaac Gibbs, Elise L. Han, Ryan J. Tibshirani, Tijana Zrnic
abstract: We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.

infographic.key_insight: Selective auditing can reduce expert review while provably keeping the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited below a user-defined threshold.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports AI decision pipelines that use confidence scores to decide when expert review is needed.
method: Receive an AI decision and a confidence score, potentially from separate models.
Choose automatic acceptance or expert review using online constrained optimization.
Apply error-control algorithms, including one that asymptotically achieves the optimal auditing rate for adversarial and i.i.d. streams.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on harmful-request screening, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling report valid error control with substantially less human auditing than baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Asymptotically optimal auditing does not ensure low review demand immediately; deployment also depends on dependable expert review capacity.
infographic.paper_title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing

title: RIDAR: Safeguarding Research Integrity in Autonomous Research Agents via Automated Detection and Runtime Intervention
authors: Jiening Siow, Amy Xin, Junjie Wang, Ziyu Tang, Zijun Yao, Yunjia Qi
abstract: Autonomous research agents are increasingly used to automate large portions of scientific research, yet they are prone to research integrity violations (RIVs): behaviors that compromise the validity, reproducibility, or faithfulness of the research process. We present RIDAR, a framework for automated RIV detection and runtime intervention. First, we introduce RIVT, a comprehensive taxonomy of 14 RIV types spanning the full research lifecycle. Building on RIVT, we present RIDAR-post-hoc, a framework to detect RIVs within agent trajectories. RIDAR-post-hoc achieves 85.2% F1 performance on RIV-Gold, a benchmark for RIV detection with 60 expert-annotated trajectories. Applying RIDAR-post-hoc to RIV-Wild, a dataset of 300 agent trajectories across 50 distinct research tasks, we detect 3,964 RIV instances in 99.7% of trajectories, revealing the prevalence of RIVs in current agents. Finally, we present RIDAR-runtime, a framework for dynamically detecting and correcting RIVs during agent runtime. RIDAR-runtime effectively reduces agent RIVs remaining at task completion by 36.8%. We will release our code and data to facilitate future research.

infographic.key_insight: RIDAR detects research integrity violations in autonomous research agents and intervenes during execution, reducing violations remaining at task completion by 36.8%.
infographic.engineering_relevance: RIDAR offers a framework for adding integrity monitoring and corrective interventions to automated scientific workflows.
method: Define 14 research integrity violation types spanning the research lifecycle in the RIVT taxonomy.
Use RIDAR-post-hoc to detect violations in recorded agent trajectories.
Use RIDAR-runtime to dynamically detect and correct violations during execution.
infographic.evidence_signal: RIDAR-post-hoc achieved 85.2% F1 on 60 expert-annotated RIV-Gold trajectories and detected 3,964 violations in 99.7% of 300 RIV-Wild trajectories across 50 research tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Runtime intervention reduces but does not eliminate violations; detection errors and intervention overhead warrant evaluation before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: RIDAR: Safeguarding Research Integrity in Autonomous Research Agents via Automated Detection and Runtime Intervention

title: SQuAT: Spherical Lattice Vector Quantization-Aware Training
authors: Sebastian Loeschcke, Ivan Koryakovskiy, Tycho F. A. van der Ouderaa, Riccardo Del Chiaro, Mart van Baalen, Paul N. Whatmough
abstract: Vector quantization (VQ), in particular lattice-based methods, offer strong rate-distortion trade-offs for low-bit large language models (LLMs), yet their behavior under quantization-aware training (VQ-QAT) remains poorly understood. We scale lattice VQ-QAT to billion-parameter LLMs and multi-billion-token training regimes, and introduce SQuAT, a shape-gain VQ-QAT approach trained with a separate straight-through estimator (STE) for the shape and gain. SQuAT decomposes weights into direction and magnitude: normalized directions are quantized using an $E_8$-derived spherical codebook, while gains are quantized independently with low-bit scalar quantizers. We show that, unlike a standard STE applied to the full quantizer, which ignores the shape-gain structure, these separate STEs induce tangent-space updates for directions, yielding an implicit form of spherical (Riemannian) optimization. To enable scalability, we develop a distributed exact nearest-neighbor assignment scheme, in which workers quantize disjoint weight blocks and communicate only discrete indices, reducing VQ-QAT training time by 12.8$\times$ and allowing us to scale it to 10B tokens. Across instruction-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen3-4B, and base Qwen3-1.7B, SQuAT consistently outperforms standard VQ-QAT STE under identical quantizers and initialization, and achieves SOTA VQ-QAT accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: SQuAT improves low-bit LLM quantization-aware training by separating weight direction and magnitude, with distinct gradient estimators that induce tangent-space updates for directions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Distributed exact nearest-neighbor assignment reduces VQ-QAT training time by 12.8×, enabling training runs of up to 10 billion tokens.
method: Decompose weight vectors into normalized directions and scalar gains.
Quantize directions with an E8-derived spherical codebook and gains with low-bit scalar quantizers, using separate straight-through estimators.
Distribute assignment across disjoint weight blocks and communicate only discrete indices.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across instruction-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B and Qwen3-4B, plus base Qwen3-1.7B, SQuAT consistently outperforms standard VQ-QAT STE with identical quantizers and initialization.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report absolute accuracy gains, hardware requirements, or inference speedups, limiting deployment-level conclusions.
infographic.paper_title: SQuAT: Spherical Lattice Vector Quantization-Aware Training

title: Diffusion Language Models for Perplexity-Aware Black-Box Attacks
authors: Ali Al-Lawati, Elsayed Eshra, Dongwon Lee, Suhang Wang
abstract: \emph{Continuous-space} attacks find prompts that trigger malicious behaviors, such as overthinking, in black-box LLMs by sampling or optimizing over a low-dimensional Gaussian latent space and decoding it to text through a \emph{random mapping} and nearest-token lookup. Because the random mapping is not learned from language, its prompts can be highly unnatural, and as such easily detectable through input guardrails, and the risk estimates they yield are not grounded in natural prompts. In this paper, we demonstrate that the same continuous latent-space framework can be coupled directly to a learned generative distribution over language, a continuous diffusion language model (dLLM), which removes the artificial random mapping while preserving the standard-Gaussian latent formulation and the downstream sampling or optimization procedure. We evaluate this approach under two settings: sampling-based estimation using \emph{RareTrap} and optimization-based search using \emph{ThinkTrap}. We find that character-level perplexity drops from $10^3$--$10^7$ to 3--5 in RareTrap and from 20--28 to 4.3--5.4 in ThinkTrap. We also find that model risk estimates can differ by an order of magnitude across the two mappings.

infographic.key_insight: Replacing a random latent-to-text mapping with a learned diffusion language model produces lower-perplexity attack prompts while preserving the continuous Gaussian latent-space framework.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Black-box LLM risk assessments can depend strongly on prompt generation, with estimated risk differing by an order of magnitude between mappings.
method: Use a continuous diffusion language model to decode standard-Gaussian latents into text.
Preserve downstream sampling and optimization procedures.
Evaluate sampling-based RareTrap and optimization-based ThinkTrap.
infographic.evidence_signal: Character-level perplexity falls from 10³–10⁷ to 3–5 in RareTrap and from 20–28 to 4.3–5.4 in ThinkTrap.
infographic.watch_item: Lower perplexity does not by itself establish guardrail evasion or representativeness of real-world prompts.
infographic.paper_title: Diffusion Language Models for Perplexity-Aware Black-Box Attacks

title: PYTHIA, a transferable machine learning framework for simultaneous defect and adsorption site optimization
authors: Ioannis Kouroudis, Zhaosu Gu, Poonam, Leon Muller, Alessio Gagliardi
abstract: Machine learning has permeated material optimization, providing high value. Nevertheless, its re- liance on a high number of samples limits its applicability to relatively explored material families. In this paper we extend the applicability of machine learning to novel and understudied materials through the PYTHIA (Probabilistic Yet Transferable Hierarchical Interaction Architecture) framework. Pythia utilizes two of the most powerful machine learning concepts, foundational models and transfer learning. We employ a complex foundational model trained on a large dataset of chemically similar molecules, on a target that is physically close to our prediction target. Then, we freeze the weights and perform subspace alignment with the use of a transformer layer and add uncertainty quantification with gaussian processes. These two layers can be trained on a limited dataset yet allow us to leverage the gained knowl- edge and the studied materials and complex architectures. The resulting model is used as a surrogate for a Bayesian Optimization scheme. To showcase the robustness of the framework, we applied it to the investigation of adsorption and defect optimization of two distinct systems. infographic.key_insight: PYTHIA transfers knowledge from a pretrained molecular model to support data-efficient, simultaneous defect and adsorption-site optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could reduce the evaluation effort needed to optimize novel or understudied materials with limited training data.
method: Pretrain a foundational model on a large dataset of chemically similar molecules using a physically related prediction target.
Freeze pretrained weights and train a transformer layer for subspace alignment, with Gaussian processes for uncertainty quantification.
Use the resulting model as a surrogate in Bayesian optimization.

infographic.watch_item: Transfer quality may depend on chemical similarity and target alignment; performance and uncertainty calibration require validation on new material families.
infographic.paper_title: PYTHIA, a transferable machine learning framework for simultaneous defect and adsorption site optimization

title: Questioning Instrumental Convergence in RLVR: Checkpoint Evidence from OLMo-3
authors: Barış Alparslan, Sandy Tanwisuth, Caleb Petterson
abstract: Instrumental convergence is often invoked as a general reason to expect capable agents to acquire or express power-seeking subgoals: self-preservation, resource acquisition, deception, or resistance to oversight which poses an important threat to the society. For LLMs, reinforcement learning is the first stage of post-training that directly optimizes behavior against an objective; therefore, it is the stage where convergent instrumental behavior, on IC grounds, likely to appear. Does reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) make a model more likely to express instrumental-convergence behavior, or does this depend on the training regime, evaluation frame, and stage of post-training? We study this question as a checkpoint-conditioned behavioral trajectory rather than as a single before/after safety score. Using InstrumentalEval, we evaluate OLMo-3-7B-Think across SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final RLVR model. The trajectory is nonmonotonic: instrumental rate rises from 25.0% at SFT to 46.1% near RLVR step 200, then falls to 11.8% at the final checkpoint. Paired item-level tests and step-wise regression support the final SFT-to-RLVR reduction. Prompt framing does not explain this pattern: a harmful-prompt indicator combined with other framing effects explains only 15% of within-checkpoint score variance on average, and Iterative Null-space Projection (INLP) removes a detectable framing direction without changing the SFT-to-final-RLVR gap. Together with preliminary 32B endpoint results (35.53% SFT to 22.37% RLVR final), these findings indicate that RLVR does not monotonically increase instrumental behavior in this setting: the rate rises early, then falls below the SFT baseline. The result is specific to this model family and benchmark, and judge agreement is moderate, so absolute rates should be read cautiously.

infographic.key_insight: On InstrumentalEval, OLMo-3-7B-Think’s instrumental behavior rose early in RLVR training, then fell below its supervised fine-tuning baseline.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate intermediate checkpoints as well as final models, because endpoint comparisons can hide transient increases in potentially risky behavior.
method: Evaluated SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final RLVR model using InstrumentalEval.
Applied paired item-level tests and step-wise regression to assess behavioral changes.
Tested prompt-framing effects and used INLP to remove a detectable framing direction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The 7B model’s instrumental rate rose from 25.0% at SFT to 46.1% near RLVR step 200, then fell to 11.8% at the final checkpoint; preliminary 32B endpoints also showed a reduction.
infographic.watch_item: Findings are specific to this model family and benchmark, and moderate judge agreement warrants caution when interpreting absolute rates.
infographic.paper_title: Questioning Instrumental Convergence in RLVR: Checkpoint Evidence from OLMo-3

title: METTA: Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning
authors: Ali Najar, Hosein Hasani, Amir Kooshan Fattah, Yasamin Rajabi, Mahdieh Soleymani Baghshah
abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to train agents that adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction, but this requires representing task evidence over long interaction histories. Classical recurrent agents compress experience into hidden states, while transformer-based agents retrieve from past trajectories at quadratic memory and computation cost. In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning. It decomposes the fast adaptation phase into two temporal scales: a causal neural memory performs fine-grained within-episode adaptation with linear sequence complexity, while compact episode-level summaries support long-range cross-episode task inference without attending over the full interaction history. Moreover, equipping agents with neural memory provides sufficient expressive capacity and test-time training capability, enabling effective adaptation to unseen held-out tasks and task families at meta-test time. On unseen held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments, METTA achieves a success rate over $50\%$ while maintaining a low training budget and short wall-clock time. On long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks, it outperforms transformer-based baselines by exhibiting more structured exploration behavior. These results show that METTA provides an efficient path toward more adaptive and scalable long-context meta-RL.

infographic.key_insight: METTA combines fine-grained neural memory with compact episode summaries to adapt to unseen tasks without attending over the full interaction history.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its two-timescale memory design offers a path to scalable long-context meta-RL with linear sequence complexity for within-episode adaptation.
method: Use causal neural memory for fine-grained within-episode adaptation.
Retain compact episode summaries for cross-episode task inference.
Enable test-time training to adapt to held-out tasks and task families.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports over 50% success on held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments and better performance than transformer baselines on long-context, sparse-reward PointMaze tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Compact episode summaries may omit useful task evidence; the abstract does not quantify this trade-off or specify exact compute budgets.
infographic.paper_title: METTA: Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning

title: On the Token Collapse Phenomenon in Textual Graph Soft Prompting
authors: Andrea Giuseppe Di Francesco, Rishabh Jain, Franco Maria Nardini, Nicola Tonellotto, Pietro Liò, Fabrizio Silvestri
abstract: Recent methods for injecting graph structure into LLM prompts include graph soft prompting, in which a graph neural network (GNN) learns graph-specific tokens that capture relational information among entities in textual prompts. G-Retriever combines graph soft prompts with a verbalized description of the same graph to strengthen the textual prompt signal. We conduct an in-depth analysis of G-Retriever and uncover a pathological behavior we term token collapse. Across three benchmarks, three graph encoders, two LLM families, and both frozen and LoRA-adapted models, G-Retriever's graph tokens become almost indistinguishable across inputs. We provide evidence that the same failure is inherited by subsequent methods, even with multi-token pooling. Under the standard setup, swapping a token with the dataset mean, a token from another example, or one derived from a corrupted graph produces no resolved answer-level effect in accuracy. Moreover, a learned constant prompt that never accesses the graph matches or surpasses G-Retriever on all three benchmarks. These findings indicate that, rather than conveying graph content as intended, the collapsed token functions primarily as a generic soft prompt. We also examine conditions linked to this collapse and propose a two-stage procedure that yields non-collapsed tokens while maintaining competitive performance in most cases. However, token variability alone does not prove that the model uses graph information: via interventions and decoding probes, we show that depending on the configuration, a token can reflect the question, an answer prior, or graph-derived content that the LLM may or may not use. Overall, our results offer a practical approach to evaluating graph-token alignment rather than inferring it from task accuracy alone. Code to reproduce our experiments is available at https://github.com/difra100/Token_Collapse_KGQA.

infographic.key_insight: G-Retriever’s graph tokens become nearly indistinguishable across inputs, functioning primarily as a generic soft prompt rather than conveying graph-specific information.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate graph-token use with controlled interventions rather than task accuracy alone, since a learned constant prompt can match or outperform graph-conditioned prompting.
method: Analyze token collapse across graph encoders, LLM families, and adaptation settings.
Replace graph tokens with dataset means, other examples’ tokens, or corrupted-graph tokens.
Test a two-stage procedure for producing non-collapsed tokens and probe what information they encode.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three benchmarks, three graph encoders, two LLM families, and frozen and LoRA-adapted models, token substitutions produced no resolved answer-accuracy effect under the standard setup.
infographic.watch_item: Non-collapsed tokens do not establish graph use: they may encode question information or answer priors, and the LLM may ignore graph-derived content.
infographic.paper_title: On the Token Collapse Phenomenon in Textual Graph Soft Prompting

title: Direct Pass@$k$ Optimization for Thought Pruning: Balancing Quality and Diversity in Test-Time Reasoning
authors: Mahdi Salmani, Adel Javanmard, Devansh Gupta, Meisam Razaviyayn
abstract: Test-time scaling has emerged as a key inference strategy for reasoning models, where a model generates a large number of candidate solutions in the hope of finding at least one correct solution. Running all candidate solutions to completion can be computationally demanding, so recent work prunes the candidate pool after generating only a short prefix, committing further computation only to the surviving candidates. Existing pruning strategies divide broadly into two categories: Quality-based methods assign a score to each partial solution and discard those predicted to ultimately lead to an incorrect final solution, while diversity-based methods select partial solutions that follow different reasoning trajectories and are therefore likely to cover different final solutions. The tension between these two objectives is an instance of exploration versus exploitation, yet little to no prior work on pruning exposes this trade-off directly, let alone optimizes it. In this paper, we introduce a pruning procedure that addresses this trade-off directly by optimizing pass@$k$ over the selected solution pool. In particular, it chooses the pool to maximize the probability that at least one of its partial solutions, when continued to completion, yields a correct answer. Because this objective simultaneously rewards high-quality partial solutions and penalizes redundancy among them, quality and diversity are naturally balanced by the criterion itself rather than through separate ad-hoc design choices. On eight open-weight reasoning models, our method outperforms existing quality-based and diversity-based pruning strategies. The gains are particularly pronounced when the pruning procedure keeps a moderate number of partial solutions for continued generation, highlighting the value of directly balancing quality and diversity during pruning.

infographic.key_insight: Directly optimizing pass@k balances candidate quality and diversity by selecting partial solutions to maximize the probability that at least one finishes correctly.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Pruning reasoning candidates after short prefixes can reduce inference computation while retaining a promising pool for continued generation.
method: Generate short prefixes for multiple candidate solutions.
Select a survivor pool by optimizing its probability of producing at least one correct completion.
Continue selected candidates, balancing quality and redundancy within one objective.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight open-weight reasoning models, the method outperforms quality-based and diversity-based pruning baselines, with especially pronounced gains when retaining a moderate number of candidates.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify how pool-level success probabilities are estimated or quantify pruning overhead, leaving deployment cost-effectiveness uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Direct Pass@$k$ Optimization for Thought Pruning: Balancing Quality and Diversity in Test-Time Reasoning

title: Evaluating the Applicability of LLM Inference Optimizations on Apple Silicon
authors: Kyrylo Yemets, Andrii Yaroshevych, Victor Muryn, Ostap Khomenko, Pavlo Kryven, Maksym Kmet
abstract: Apple Silicon is among the most widely used platforms for local LLM inference, yet nearly all inference optimizations are designed and validated on server-class NVIDIA GPUs under batched serving workloads. Which optimizations retain their benefits when moved to Apple Silicon, and what determines their applicability? We evaluate four optimization families: KV-cache pruning, speculative decoding, ported GPU kernels, and post-training quantization. Experiments span four Apple machines under a common single-request decode workload, with matched RTX 4090 comparisons where possible. KV-cache pruning can reach up to 1.75 times end-to-end throughput on Apple but can reduce throughput on desktop NVIDIA GPUs. Under the common benchmark, all evaluated speculative decoding methods reduce throughput on Apple, despite reported 2-6 times gains on server GPUs. CUDA kernel designs transfer only partially: public Metal lacks asynchronous copy, and batch-one decode makes several serving-oriented mechanisms inapplicable, although transferable components yield up to 1.20 times decode throughput. Quantization gains vary by machine. Across four families, a reported speedup is not a portable property of a technique alone but a joint function of technique, runtime, hardware contract, and workload regime.

infographic.key_insight: LLM inference speedups are not portable by default: benefits depend jointly on the technique, runtime, hardware capabilities, and workload.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For local Apple Silicon inference, benchmark optimizations under single-request decoding rather than assuming server-GPU gains will transfer.
method: Evaluate KV-cache pruning, speculative decoding, ported GPU kernels, and post-training quantization.
Use a common single-request decode workload across four Apple machines.
Compare with matched RTX 4090 runs where possible.
infographic.evidence_signal: KV-cache pruning reached up to 1.75× end-to-end throughput on Apple and transferable kernel components up to 1.20× decode throughput, while all evaluated speculative decoding methods reduced throughput under the common benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: Public Metal lacks asynchronous copy, and batch-one decoding makes several serving-oriented mechanisms inapplicable; quantization gains also vary by machine.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluating the Applicability of LLM Inference Optimizations on Apple Silicon

title: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification
authors: Sachin Gupta
abstract: Wrong automatic routing of an IT support ticket can cost more than human triage. We evaluate cost-aware abstention as an offline, cost-conditional readiness assessment: select a routing policy on calibration data under explicit costs, then evaluate that frozen policy once on held-out test data. On a public 47,837-ticket, eight-class corpus, we compare four trained non-LLM classifiers with four large language models under zero- and few-shot prompting. Under the illustrative cost model (c_ok, c_triage, c_wrong) = (0, 1, 5), TF-IDF with logistic regression and a threshold of 0.60 selected on calibration reduces test cost from 0.763 to 0.472, a 38.1% relative reduction (paired ratio-bootstrap 95% CI [35.7%, 40.4%]), while lowering wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%. Frozen calibration-selected policies also beat both always-route and always-defer on held-out test data in 14 of 16 settings in a post-hoc cost-parameter analysis. The strongest prompted configuration reaches 0.477 accuracy on a stratified 1,000-ticket test subset, versus 0.879 for fine-tuned DistilBERT on the same tickets. Isotonic lowers expected calibration error without reliably improving discrimination: GPT-4o-mini few-shot has one confidence value before and after recalibration and correctness AUROC 0.500. We therefore report correctness AUROC and tie-aware risk-coverage area alongside ECE. At the analytically derived break-even probability 0.80, seven prompted configurations defer all tickets; Haiku few-shot routes only 19/1,000. An LLM-only agreement control and margin/entropy rejection baselines further separate calibration from discrimination. The findings are scoped to this dataset, prompt design, model endpoints, and illustrative costs; the work is an evaluation framework, not a new abstention algorithm or universal deployment certification.

infographic.key_insight: Under illustrative routing costs, calibration-selected abstention cut TF-IDF logistic regression’s held-out test cost by 38.1% and reduced wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Cost-aware deferral can help determine when automatic ticket routing is preferable to human triage, but confidence calibration alone does not establish routing readiness.
method: Compare four trained non-LLM classifiers with four LLMs using zero- and few-shot prompts.
Select routing policies on calibration data under explicit costs, then freeze them for held-out testing.
Assess calibration and discrimination using ECE, correctness AUROC, and tie-aware risk-coverage area.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a public 47,837-ticket, eight-class corpus, the cost reduction had a 95% bootstrap CI of 35.7%–40.4%; on a stratified 1,000-ticket subset, the strongest prompted configuration achieved 0.477 accuracy versus DistilBERT’s 0.879.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on the dataset, prompts, model endpoints, and illustrative costs; this framework is not universal deployment certification.
infographic.paper_title: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

title: Certified Execution Harness for Agentic AI: Safe and Least-Intrusive Petri-Net Supervisory Control Between Reasoning and Action
authors: Chao Gu, Quanyan Zhu
abstract: This paper studies the problem of safe tool execution for large language model (LLM) agents under prompt injection. Using Petri nets, we formalize the execution harness between the LLM and its tools as a supervisory control problem, in which marks represent capabilities, approvals and budgets. Since a transition fires only if the marks it needs are present, an injected request whose preconditions are unmet or already spent is refused regardless of its wording. Treating tool outcomes as uncontrollable, we enforce safety by the conventional maximally permissive supervisor, and this safety transfers to the running system under four assumptions. Moreover, to capture an agent that may propose again after a refusal, we introduce the notion of a replanning closed loop, in which each retry costs an inference call. We show that, in this loop, the conventional supervisor can be arbitrarily more intrusive than a stricter safe one. Furthermore, for a given proposer model, the maximally permissive least-intrusive supervisor is characterized as a value-threshold refinement of the conventional one. Under precise conditions, this refinement orders two concurrent actions by at most one monitor place. On an autonomous release agent, we find by synthesis that safe deployment requires a step that the supervisor can refuse after a rollout starts.

infographic.key_insight: A Petri-net execution harness can block unsafe agent tool calls, but allowing every safe action need not minimize costly replanning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Encoding capabilities, approvals, and budgets as execution preconditions makes tool-call authorization independent of injected wording.
method: Model tool execution as Petri-net supervisory control, treating tool outcomes as uncontrollable.
Analyze a replanning closed loop where each retry incurs an inference call.
Refine the conventional safe supervisor using value thresholds to minimize intrusiveness for a given proposer model.
infographic.evidence_signal: Formal analysis shows the conventional supervisor can be arbitrarily more intrusive than a stricter safe supervisor; synthesis on an autonomous release agent identifies a necessary refusal-capable step after rollout begins.
infographic.watch_item: Safety transfer to the running system depends on four assumptions, while least-intrusive control depends on the chosen proposer model.
infographic.paper_title: Certified Execution Harness for Agentic AI: Safe and Least-Intrusive Petri-Net Supervisory Control Between Reasoning and Action

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
authors: Qijin Zhang, Hanzhen Wang, Yuehan Zhao, Haoyu Dai, Yao Shu, Zhongxiang Dai
abstract: Tool-using language model agents rely on environmental facts to decide whether an action is permitted. When a tool response omits a safety-relevant fact, an agent may carry out a prohibited action even though the user request is benign and every returned statement is true. We introduce \bench{}, an executable benchmark for evaluating unsafe execution, safety boundaries, and evidence recovery in LLM agents under missing evidence. It contains 300 matched unsafe/safe task pairs across six domains. By systematically suppressing critical facts, the benchmark measures unsafe execution under critical evidence omission and determines the minimum observed failure cardinality, including failures with full evidence and cases with no observed failure after exhaustive testing. An independent audit tool tests whether agents seek missing facts and then withhold prohibited actions while completing permissible tasks. The benchmark reveals substantial variation across the ten models in omission robustness, evidence acquisition, and appropriate action. Resistance to missing evidence does not necessarily translate into useful recovery. Recovery access reduces unsafe execution for all ten models, but agents differ in whether they actively obtain the missing facts and use them to act appropriately in both worlds.

infographic.key_insight: LLM agents can execute prohibited actions when tool responses omit safety-critical facts, even if the user request is benign and every returned statement is true.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Safety-sensitive agent workflows should support explicit evidence recovery and verify that recovered facts guide both safe refusal and permissible task completion.
method: Evaluate 300 matched unsafe/safe task pairs across six domains.
Systematically suppress critical facts to measure unsafe execution and the minimum observed omission count triggering failure.
Use an independent audit tool to test evidence acquisition and appropriate action.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across ten models, recovery access reduced unsafe execution for every model, but evidence acquisition and appropriate action varied substantially.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness to missing evidence does not guarantee useful recovery; evaluate both prohibited-action avoidance and permissible-task completion.
infographic.paper_title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence

title: PhysTrace: Interpretable Temporal Evaluation of Physical Consistency in Video Generative Models
authors: Taekoan Yoo, Wonkyung Jung, Kyunghun Kim, Kyeongbo Kong
abstract: World action models increasingly rely on pretrained video models assumed to capture physical dynamics for prediction, planning, and action generation. Existing evaluations assess plausibility, probe representations, or measure predictive surprise, but rarely identify which history-conditioned physical expectations conflict with observations. We introduce PhysTrace, a training-free framework aligning MLLM-generated, history-conditioned expectations with observed video windows to temporally localize physical violations and provide interpretable descriptions without task-specific probes or classifiers. We also introduce IntPhys2-Timing, adding violation intervals to IntPhys2. PhysTrace achieves a Hit Rate of up to 70.7% across physical principles on IntPhys2-Timing and outperforms the compared methods in overall possible-impossible discrimination accuracy on IntPhys2. Applied to reconstructed videos along the trajectories of pretrained diffusion/flow-based video models, PhysTrace reveals attribute- and noise-dependent patterns in physical violation localization, enabling interpretable physical consistency analysis across timesteps.

infographic.key_insight: PhysTrace pinpoints when video observations conflict with history-conditioned physical expectations and explains the violations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can help engineers diagnose physical inconsistencies in video models used for prediction, planning, and action generation.
method: Generate history-conditioned physical expectations with a multimodal large language model.
Align expectations with observed video windows to localize and describe violations without task-specific training.
Analyze reconstructed videos across diffusion and flow model trajectories.
infographic.evidence_signal: On IntPhys2-Timing, which adds violation intervals to IntPhys2, PhysTrace achieves up to 70.7% Hit Rate across physical principles; on IntPhys2, it outperforms compared methods in overall possible–impossible discrimination accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Reliance on MLLM-generated expectations warrants validation beyond the reported benchmarks before use in safety-critical planning.
infographic.paper_title: PhysTrace: Interpretable Temporal Evaluation of Physical Consistency in Video Generative Models

title: Fine-Grained Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Learning via Algorithmic Stability
authors: Guodong Zheng, Yan Sun, Peng Wang, Enneng Yang, Jiafei Lyu, Xiaochun Cao
abstract: Understanding catastrophic forgetting, in which learning new tasks degrades performance on previously learned tasks, remains a fundamental challenge in continual learning (CL). Existing theoretical analyses often rely on specific model or task structures and offer limited insight into how iterative optimization affects forgetting. To address this gap, we develop an algorithmic stability framework for expected population forgetting under SGD without prescribing a particular model architecture. Specifically, we decompose forgetting into intra-task and cross-task generalization gaps and empirical forgetting. To bound the generalization gaps, we track how a sample perturbation affects updates within a task and propagates through subsequent tasks. We consider constant, intra-task decaying, and continuously decaying learning-rate schedules. Comparing the two decaying schedules allows us to characterize how restarting learning-rate decay at task boundaries affects the propagation of historical sample perturbations. For empirical forgetting, we derive bounds for all three schedules by retaining cumulative gradient alignment along the optimization trajectory, without requiring convexity. Combining these results yields upper bounds on expected forgetting that capture the effects of training set size, the number of updates per task, the total number of tasks, learning-rate schedules, and cumulative gradient alignment. Finally, we conduct experiments on Split CIFAR-100 and Split MiniImageNet to examine the empirical implications of our theoretical findings.

infographic.key_insight: An algorithmic stability framework bounds expected catastrophic forgetting under SGD by tracking sample-perturbation propagation and cumulative gradient alignment across tasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The bounds clarify how dataset size, updates per task, task count, and learning-rate schedules influence forgetting in continual-learning systems.
method: Decompose forgetting into intra-task and cross-task generalization gaps plus empirical forgetting.
Track sample perturbations under constant, task-restarted decaying, and continuously decaying learning rates.
Bound empirical forgetting using cumulative gradient alignment without requiring convexity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on Split CIFAR-100 and Split MiniImageNet examine the empirical implications of the theoretical findings.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative results, so it does not establish which learning-rate schedule performs best in practice.
infographic.paper_title: Fine-Grained Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Learning via Algorithmic Stability

title: RheOPT: Few-Shot Non-Newtonian Flow Prediction via Newtonian Pretraining of RheOFormer
authors: Maedeh Saberi, Amir Barati Farimani, Safa Jamali
abstract: Despite advances in numerical methods, non-Newtonian flow simulations remain computationally expensive because velocity and stress must be advanced together through rate- and history-dependent constitutive dynamics. Neural-operator surrogates reduce inference cost after training, but their training data require the same expensive simulations they aim to replace, making data-efficient learning essential when only a few non-Newtonian simulations can be afforded. Here, we introduce the Rheological Operator Pretrained Transformer (RheOPT), which pretrains a transformer-based neural operator on inexpensive Newtonian simulations and fine-tunes it on a small number of non-Newtonian samples. Rather than transferring the Newtonian constitutive response itself, RheOPT reuses geometry-conditioned transport structure that remains useful after the stress model changes. We evaluate RheOPT in two geometry-matched settings: a $4{:}1$ contraction channel for Giesekus, Oldroyd-B, and Bingham fluids, and the oscillatory wake behind a triangular obstacle for Oldroyd-B flow. In the contraction, Newtonian pretraining substantially improves few-shot prediction, and a model fine-tuned on four target samples can match or exceed a from-scratch model trained on four times as many. This benefit is reliable under reversible instance normalization (RevIN) but dataset dependent under Global normalization, a difference we trace to the dynamic range of each fluid's velocity and stress fields. In the wake, where relative $L_2$ error alone cannot verify that vortex shedding is recovered, phase-insensitive diagnostics show that pretraining recovers the shedding frequency and wake fluctuation amplitude that are suppressed by the from-scratch model in the few-shot regime. Overall, RheOPT establishes Newtonian simulation as a physically grounded pretraining source for data-efficient non-Newtonian operator learning.

infographic.key_insight: RheOPT transfers geometry-conditioned transport structure from Newtonian simulations to improve non-Newtonian flow prediction with few target samples.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Pretraining on inexpensive Newtonian simulations can reduce the costly non-Newtonian training data needed for neural-operator surrogates.
method: Pretrain a transformer-based neural operator on Newtonian flow simulations.
Fine-tune on a few non-Newtonian samples in matched geometries.
Evaluate field prediction and phase-insensitive wake dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across contraction and triangular-obstacle wake tests, four-sample fine-tuning can match or exceed 16-sample training from scratch in the contraction, while wake diagnostics show recovered shedding frequency and fluctuation amplitude.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer gains depend on normalization: they are reliable with RevIN but dataset dependent with Global normalization; geometry-mismatched transfer is not established.
infographic.paper_title: RheOPT: Few-Shot Non-Newtonian Flow Prediction via Newtonian Pretraining of RheOFormer

title: SpectralCanary: Embarrassingly Simple Low-Frequency Traces for T2I Dataset-Use Auditing
authors: Sy-Tuyen Ho, Anirudh Satheesh, Soham Chawathe, Huy Nghiem, Yongkyun Lee, Andrew Adams Schoen
abstract: Auditing whether a text-to-image (T2I) model was fine-tuned on a particular image collection is difficult: a model can absorb collection-level visual characteristics without reproducing training images. Proactive dataset-use auditing plants a shared signal in a dataset before release, then later checks whether that signal appears in a suspect model's generated outputs. Existing approaches often trade off verifiability, fidelity, robustness, and deployability. We introduce $\textbf{SpectralCanary}$, which uses a smooth low-pass mask to blend a fixed canary image into every collection image while leaving captions unchanged and requiring neither auxiliary generation nor per-image optimization. A lightweight verifier detects the transferred signal in suspect-model outputs. Across eight tests on the Pokemon dataset and three realistic data transformations, spanning two architectures families, SpectralCanary achieves the highest average per-generation TPR@$1\%$ FPR ($91.1\%$) and fixed threshold model-level accuracy using 30 generations ($94.8\%$) among the evaluated methods. Across five datasets spanning artistic, medical, satellite, and fashion domains with SD3.5, SpectralCanary averages $92.4\%$ per-generation TPR@$1\%$ FPR while preserving the released images (SSIM $0.989$, LPIPS $0.022$) with a near-zero mean change FID (mean $Δ$FID $0.05$) across datasets. Matched-energy ablations on Pokemon and ROCOv2 support our design choice, low-frequency placement transfers more reliably compared to mid/high-frequency placement. Under the evaluated adaptive attacks, the most effective removal requires aggressive modification and incurs more than $25$ $Δ$FID points. These results identify low-frequency visual signals as effective carriers for collection-level T2I audit traces.

infographic.key_insight: SpectralCanary embeds a shared low-frequency visual trace into an image collection so its use in text-to-image fine-tuning can later be audited through generated outputs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables lightweight dataset-use auditing without changing captions, generating auxiliary images, or optimizing each image individually.
method: Blend a fixed canary image into collection images using a smooth low-pass mask.
Release the modified images with unchanged captions.
Use a lightweight verifier to detect the transferred trace in suspect-model generations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five datasets with SD3.5, the method averaged 92.4% per-generation TPR at 1% FPR, with released-image SSIM of 0.989, LPIPS of 0.022, and mean ΔFID of 0.05.
infographic.watch_item: Auditing requires marking the collection before release; robustness beyond the evaluated architectures, transformations, and adaptive attacks remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: SpectralCanary: Embarrassingly Simple Low-Frequency Traces for T2I Dataset-Use Auditing

title: Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration
authors: Deepthika S, Pawni Yadav, B. Sankar
abstract: Research on sycophancy asks whether large language models (LLMs) bend towards what their users want to hear. We ask the reverse question: when an LLM is confident, consistent, and wrong, do users bend towards it? In a within-subjects experiment, 32 participants learned up to five science topics by chatting with five assistants built on the same model (GPT-5-mini). Unknown to participants, each assistant's briefing had 0, 25, 50, 75, or 100% of its facts replaced by plausible falsehoods, and every assistant spoke with full confidence. A surprise quiz after each topic offered the correct fact, the planted falsehood, and two distractors, with a confidence rating for every answer. Across 104 quizzes and 1,040 answers, scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10, and the planted option was chosen on 60% of falsified items against 11% of correctly taught ones (odds ratio 12.5). Transcript coding showed that whenever the assistant stated a falsehood, it was adopted about 65% of the time at every falsification level. Absorbed falsehoods were held with high confidence (8.4/10), the modeled confidence advantage of right over wrong answers vanished, and the discrimination of confidence for correctness fell from an AUROC of 0.70 to chance, while post-task trust ratings barely moved. Participants tended to return to the chat more when the assistant was worse, but returning went with more absorption, not less, and 30% of all turns pasted quiz questions back to the source being checked. The assistant itself was almost never sycophantic and never conceded under pushback. We introduce a baseline-corrected Human Deference Index to quantify this human-side sycophancy and argue that trustworthiness is a property of the human-AI pair, that sycophancy evaluations should measure both directions, and that learning interfaces must make reliability legible claim by claim.

infographic.key_insight: Confidently wrong LLMs can draw users toward false beliefs while leaving trust largely unchanged and eroding their ability to distinguish correct from incorrect answers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learning interfaces should make claim-level reliability visible and support independent verification rather than treating confident delivery or user trust as evidence of accuracy.
method: Within-subjects study: 32 participants learned up to five science topics with assistants built on GPT-5-mini.
Assistant briefings contained 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100% plausible falsehoods, all delivered confidently.
Surprise quizzes, answer-confidence ratings, transcript coding, and a baseline-corrected Human Deference Index assessed human-side deference.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 104 quizzes and 1,040 answers, scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10; planted falsehood selection rose from 11% on correctly taught items to 60% on falsified items, while confidence discrimination fell from AUROC 0.70 to chance.
infographic.watch_item: The small, single-model science-learning study with deliberately manipulated briefings may not generalize to other users, domains, or naturally occurring model errors.
infographic.paper_title: Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration

title: Social-HUMINT: An LLM-Augmented Unified Framework for Measuring Social Media Exposure
authors: Pellegrino Casoria, Simon Pietro Romano
abstract: In the post-API landscape, social-media profiling has become inexpensive and automated: Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract structured information from unstructured content and deduce attributes users never disclosed. A person's true exposure is not what they post but what can be inferred from it. As these practices become routine, exposure to social engineering attacks becomes an operational certainty, demanding a shared framework for assessment and mitigation. We make this exposure measurable by quantifying how accurately a target can be profiled, and how far that profile enables social engineering attacks. Because no existing model fully spans this continuum, we unify Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) and Cyber Human Intelligence (Cyber-HUMINT), two individual-focused disciplines that evolved separately, into a single doctrine-grounded taxonomy of 38 capabilities across the Cyber Threat Intelligence lifecycle, where user profiling bridges passive collection and active engagement. Domain experts validated the taxonomy (Fleiss' $κ$ = 0.92). We operationalize its core path (extraction, inference, and susceptibility assessment) as an LLM-augmented multi-agent pipeline, evaluated on real participants' public data. Susceptibility is assessed indirectly: the pipeline predicts how each target would rank personalized engagement options, matching their actual choices significantly above chance. This ranking capacity captures the personalization on which tailored attacks depend. The underlying profiles are accurate: extraction reaches F1 = 97.3%, and inferred attributes score 4.73/5, both far above rule-based and NER-based baselines at negligible cost. The framework augments security analysts' tradecraft rather than replacing it and enables defenders to gauge their own exposure before an adversary does.

infographic.key_insight: Social-HUMINT measures social-media exposure through both accurate user profiling and the personalization that could enable social engineering.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Security teams can use the framework to assess inferable personal information and prioritize exposure mitigation before adversaries exploit it.
method: Unify SOCMINT and Cyber-HUMINT into 38 capabilities across the Cyber Threat Intelligence lifecycle.
Use an LLM-augmented multi-agent pipeline for extraction, inference, and susceptibility assessment.
Predict participants’ rankings of personalized engagement options and compare them with actual choices.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on real participants’ public data reported extraction F1 of 97.3%, inferred-attribute scores of 4.73/5, above-chance ranking predictions, and expert taxonomy agreement of Fleiss’ κ = 0.92.
infographic.watch_item: Susceptibility is measured indirectly through engagement rankings, not observed success of real social-engineering attacks.
infographic.paper_title: Social-HUMINT: An LLM-Augmented Unified Framework for Measuring Social Media Exposure
